grades.quote: The fact that sleep holds one or the other of these locks at all times is what prevents a concurrent wakeup (which must acquire and hold both) from acting, and thus prevents a lost wake-up.
grades.reason: Explains how sleep/wakeup locking (holding the condition lock or p->lock from before the condition check until the process is marked SLEEPING) prevents a lost wake-up. This gives the mechanism that was violated when a sleeper misses an earlier wakeup. It is less direct than a definition of the symptom.

grades.quote: A thread that finds circumstances not to its liking executes the wait operation and thereby goes to sleep until such time as another thread invokes the notify operation.
grades.reason: Generic introduction to condition variables (wait/notify) with a bounded-buffer example. It does not discuss lost wakeups or why a waiter could sleep forever after the notify already ran, so it only gives background.

grades.quote: wait_lock (2503), which acts as the condition lock that helps ensure that kwait doesn’t miss a wakeup from an exiting child.
grades.reason: Applies the condition-lock idea to wait/exit, noting that wait_lock prevents a parent from losing a wakeup from an exiting child. It is a specific application and does not address the general diagnosis.

grades.quote: A call to wakeup at that point would find no sleeping process to wake up; the wakeup would simply return. But then the call to sleep might never wake up, since the wakeup intended for it has already happened. This undesirable situation is called a _lost wake-up_ .
grades.reason: Directly describes this scenario. A wakeup that runs between the condition check and the call to sleep finds nobody to wake, so the sleeper sleeps forever. This is a lost wake-up. It also gives the fix: hold the condition lock and pass it to sleep, so release and sleep are atomic with respect to wakeup.
